report.tagline: An app and account for sending, holding and spending money in other currencies at the real exchange rate with a small, upfront fee.
report.simpleSummary: Wise lets you send money abroad cheaply. When you send £1,000 from London to your parents in India, Wise shows the exact fee and the exact rupees they will get before you pay. It uses the real market exchange rate, not a worse rate with a hidden markup like most banks. You can also hold 40+ currencies in one account and spend them with a Wise debit card when you travel.

overview.whatItDoes: Wise moves money between countries and currencies for people and businesses. It charges a visible fee and uses the mid-market rate, which is the rate you see on Google. It also gives you an account with local bank details in several countries and a debit card. Banks and apps can also plug into Wise's network through Wise Platform.
howItWorks: You enter how much you want to send and see the fee, the rate and the arrival time before you pay.

Wise rarely moves money across borders for each transfer. It holds money in local bank accounts in each country, takes your pounds in the UK and pays rupees out of its Indian pool, so the money never actually crosses the border.
Because it matches flows in both directions, it avoids slow and costly correspondent bank chains, and many transfers arrive in seconds.
The multi-currency account gives you local details (for example a UK sort code, a US routing number, a euro IBAN) so you can get paid like a local.
The Wise card spends from whichever currency balance you hold, and converts at the real rate if you do not have the right currency.
Wise Platform lets banks such as Morgan Stanley and Standard Chartered offer Wise transfers inside their own apps.
overview.valueProposition: You keep more of your money when it crosses borders, and you know exactly what will arrive and when, before you press send.

businessModel.summary: Wise makes money from three things: a small fee on each transfer or conversion, a cut of card payments, and interest earned on customer money it holds. It deliberately cuts prices as its costs fall, so it grows by being cheaper than everyone else.

revenueStreams.detail: A percentage fee plus a small fixed fee on each transfer. The average take rate (the share of each transfer Wise keeps) is roughly 0.5% to 0.6%, and lower for popular routes and large amounts.
Interchange, a small fee paid by the shop's bank each time the card is used, plus conversion fees on card spend.
Wise earns interest on the billions customers hold. It passes some back to customers and keeps the rest. This grew fast while interest rates were high.
Business account fees, and fees from banks that use Wise Platform.

businessModel.pricing: Free to sign up. Transfer fees start from about 0.33% depending on currency route; sending pounds to rupees is typically around 0.5% to 0.7% of the amount plus a small fixed fee. Card is a one-time fee of about £7 in the UK. Two free ATM withdrawals up to £200 a month, then a fee. Prices change often, so check the live calculator.
costDrivers: Compliance and fraud checks: identity verification, anti-money-laundering teams and tools, in every country
Banking partners and payment network fees in each local market
Customer support for held or delayed transfers
Engineering for its own payment network and direct links to central bank payment systems
Marketing, though most growth comes from word of mouth
businessModel.unitEconomics: Take one £1,000 transfer from the UK to India. Wise keeps roughly £5 to £6 in fees. Moving the money costs it maybe £1 to £2, because it pays out from rupees already sitting in India. The rest pays for compliance, support and profit. A regular customer sending £1,000 every month earns Wise about £60 to £70 a year from transfers alone, plus card fees and interest on any balance they keep. Since most customers arrive through word of mouth, the cost to get a customer is low, so each one is profitable quickly.

howTheyGetUsers: Word of mouth: Wise says most new customers come from recommendations
Referral programme with a reward for each friend who makes a transfer
Price comparison pages that rank well in search for 'send money to India' and similar
Banks and fintechs using Wise Platform, which bring Wise volume without a Wise sign-up
Students and migrants who are told about it by communities and universities
whatBringsUsersBack: Monthly remittances are a natural repeat habit
Money held in balances earns interest and stays in the app
Card spending on trips and online in other currencies
Repeat recipients saved, so the next transfer takes a few taps
Rate alerts that pull users back when the rate moves
growth.moat: Wise has built its own payment network over 15 years: local accounts in dozens of countries, licences in each, and direct links to central bank payment systems in places like the UK, Singapore and Brazil. This makes its cost per transfer lower than rivals, and it passes the savings on as lower prices, which brings more volume, which lowers costs again. A new rival would need years of licences and partnerships to match it.

competitors.name: Banks (HSBC, Barclays, SBI)
competitors.positioning: Already hold your money, so transfers are convenient but expensive.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Wise is usually several times cheaper and faster, and shows the true cost upfront.

competitors.name: Remitly
competitors.positioning: Remittances focused on migrants sending money home, with cash pickup and mobile wallets.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Remitly often uses promotional rates for new users. Wise wins on transparent pricing and on accounts and cards, not just transfers.

competitors.name: Revolut
competitors.positioning: All-in-one money app with fee-free conversion within plan limits.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Revolut is cheaper on weekdays inside limits but adds markups on weekends and above limits. Wise is focused on doing cross-border well, with clearer pricing for large amounts.

competitors.name: Western Union
competitors.positioning: Old global brand with a huge cash network.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Western Union reaches people without bank accounts. Wise is digital-only and much cheaper for bank-to-bank transfers.

competitors.name: PayPal and Xoom
competitors.positioning: Pay people and get paid online globally.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: PayPal's currency conversion includes a markup of about 3 to 4%. Freelancers often move to Wise to keep more of each payment.

northStar.metric: Cross-border volume moved for active customers, at a falling average price
northStar.why: Volume shows how much money customers trust Wise with. Pairing it with a falling price keeps the team honest: Wise only wins if customers keep more of their money. Revenue alone could grow by raising prices, which would break the mission.

Profitable at scale, with a 20 to 25% target margin

pmLessons: Pricing can be the product. Wise turned 'show the real fee' into its whole brand, and that trust drives word of mouth.
Cost advantage compounds. Every saving passed back to users brings more volume, which makes the next saving possible.
In money products, safety checks are part of the experience. A frozen account is a product failure even when compliance is right.
A repeat habit like monthly remittances is worth more than one big transaction.

interviewQuestions.question: Wise's profit relies partly on interest income. What would you do as rates fall?
interviewQuestions.hint: Split revenue into fees, cards and interest. Suggest ways to grow fee volume (business, Platform) and card habit. Talk about trade-offs between price cuts and margin.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you reduce complaints about frozen accounts without raising fraud?
interviewQuestions.hint: Clarify the user types affected. Map the hold journey. Propose clear status, document checklists and risk-based tiers. Guardrail: fraud loss rate.

interviewQuestions.question: Should Wise launch in India for Indian residents? How would you decide?
interviewQuestions.hint: Look at market size (inbound remittances over $120bn), regulation (RBI rules, LRS limits), competition (banks, UPI), and what Wise uniquely offers. Pick a narrow first use case.

interviewQuestions.question: Design a feature to win more freelancers from PayPal.
interviewQuestions.hint: Define the freelancer's pain: fees, slow access, invoices. Ideas: invoice links, client-pays-in-local-currency, tax summaries. Metric: monthly inbound volume per freelancer.

interviewQuestions.question: What north star metric would you pick for Wise and why?
interviewQuestions.hint: Pick something that shows value to users: volume moved at falling price, or money saved versus banks. Explain why revenue is a bad north star here.

glossary.meaning: The real exchange rate halfway between the buy and sell prices, the one you see on Google.
The share of each transaction's value that a company keeps as revenue.
A small fee the shop's bank pays the card issuer every time a card is used.
The share of customers who keep using a product over time.
The one number a company uses to measure the value it delivers to users.
A middle bank that passes an international payment between two banks that have no direct link.
A way for one company's software to talk to another's, so a bank can use Wise inside its own app.

assumptions: FY26 revenue, profit and balance figures come from a summary of the results release and may differ slightly from the full report.
The £5 to £6 fee on a £1,000 UK to India transfer is an estimate based on typical published pricing; actual fees vary by route and payment method.
The cost to Wise of each transfer is our inference, not a reported figure.
Take rate of about 0.5% to 0.6% is based on recent reported averages and may have moved.
